January 9
Epiphany 1C — The First Sunday of Epiphany [Baptism of our Lord]
Color: white, gold
Isaiah 42:1-9
Psalm 89:1-29, alt: Psalm 89:20-29
Acts 10:34-38
Mt 3:13-17


Grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ - Lord and Creator of all there was and ever will be. Surprise!


The season of Christmas is over, and we have moved on into Epiphany. The Feast of Epiphany was January 6 (also the 24 anniversary of my ordination) and is traditionally celebrated by the reading from the 2nd chapter of Matthew in which the Magi visit the newborn Jesus. An epiphany, in general, is a startling insight, a blazing glimpse of the not-so-obvious. I can hardly quibble with the Gospel reading selected for this day, but it seems to me the Magi were quite deliberate in seeking out Jesus. By the time you get to the end of the reading, we find two epiphanic moments.


I had been doing some reading about the Holy Spirit because I had been writing something else and found my actual knowledge (as opposed to my assumed knowledge) of the Holy Spirit was sadly lacking. This led me to read about the Doctrine of Creation and some truly fascinating stuff - at least fascinating for a light-middleweight theologian. Stuff I had not bothered to think about a whole lot. Stuff that I REALLY wanted to write about for you all, but I thought it was irrelevant to The Epiphany. Or so I thought.


Without getting too deep into the weeds, The first thing I learned was that if you trust that Jesus is God, it necessarily follows that God the Father created a complete, consistent, and completely separate thing from himself. This means that Creation is a trustworthy witness to itself. It also means that Creation is itself a witness to the Creator, God the Father. Not a witness in the sense that we can look at Jesus and see the Father, but in the sense of *WHOA! God really passed by here!*. St. Paul affirms this when he writes to the Romans, 
    For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made... (Romans 1:20)


So, I fretted over whether to write about this neat stuff I learned about Creation or the epiphanies of the Magi. Of course, as it turns out, there is a connection. St. Matthew tells us that wise men from the east came to Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of Jews. They came because they "saw his star rising." What-ho!?! The Magi observe a natural phenomenon and take that as a sign (or witness) that a new king has been born to the Jews.


There are some things we can assume about the Magi that St. Matthew does not explicitly tell us. The Magi were not likely Jewish - had they been, they would not have had to journey from the East to Jerusalem. The Magi were reasonably well-read; after all, they knew about the kings of Israel and that Israel lived in expectation of a Messiah. However, we find the Magi were not as well read as the Scribes and the Pharisees since they hadn't figured out the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem. Furthermore, their expectation was that the Messiah would be in Jerusalem.


The Magi and their entourage (one does not make long journeys with gold, frankincense, and myrrh in the bad 'ol days without escort) arrive in Jerusalem and naively ask, "We would like to pay homage to the Messiah; where can we find him?" No doubt, the expectation of the Magi was a young king in a manner after David or Solomon, and knowledge of his whereabouts widely known. As it turned out, no one knew what they were talking about, but that didn't keep their arrival and question from quickly turning into the talk of the town. 


We should not be surprised that (supposed) King Herod considered the birth of the Messiah as a threat to his rule - no doubt he also considered the Messiah to be like David or Solomon. He secretly summons the Magi and sends them on a secret mission of state to locate the newborn Messiah.


Bethlehem is a short distance from Jerusalem, hardly a good day's walk and probably had a population of around 300, about 50-60 households. It would not have been an onerous task to knock on all the doors looking for newborn messiahs. Even so, upon arriving in Bethlehem, the Magi once again find natural phenomena bearing witness to the location. Just seeing the star caused them great joy, possibly along the lines of *Zoinks! We were right!* Bear in mind they hadn't even seen the young Messiah yet. But upon entering the household and seeing Mary with the child-king, they fell down and worshipped him. 


So far, the Magi have had several epiphanies: a couple of natural, astronomical phenomena bearing witness to the Messiah's birth; actually meeting young Jesus and intuiting he was the Messiah; the actual Messiah was not what they had expected. The epiphanies are not over for the Magi. In a dream, the Magi are warned not to return to Herod. Surprise of surprises, it turns out Herod is not so much interested in worship as he is in murder.


What can we learn from this story? First of all, Creation does bear witness to its creator, God the Father. It bears witness in the sense of *God was here and did this and moved on*. The second thing we can learn is Jesus is not the kind of king people expected (or do expect) him to be. He comes with the positive attributes of David and Solomon without the downside. The last thing I will mention is in spite of St. Paul saying
    Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. (Romans 13:1)
He does not mean governing authorities are friends of God. History teaches that in spite of being instituted by God, governing authorities rarely, if ever, acknowledge who they are responsible to.


Now, this should come as no surprise, and yet somehow, we tend to be surprised. Keep foremost in your mind that Jesus is God, we are subject to his rule, and his rule given by his Father, for the benefit of all Creation.


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always. 
paul+
